assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson and Tabellini turned political economics into a systematic, testable field. They study how electoral rules, constitutions and forms of government shape fiscal policy and public goods. Besley adds work on state capacity, accountability and political selection. The theory and the empirical work both shaped later research in public economics, development and comparative politics. The field is distinct from, and complements, the 2024 institutions prize.
assessment.attribution: The core is the Persson-Tabellini programme (the book and the papers on constitutions and fiscal outcomes). Besley is a close contributor through state capacity (with Persson) and political agency. Others, such as Alesina and Drazen, also made related contributions, so a three-person limit leaves some credit disputes.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key work dates from the mid-1990s to the 2010s, with substantial replication and extension. The Committee can judge lasting influence with confidence.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions could count against it.
Credit relative to Alesina, Drazen, Acemoglu and others who worked on adjacent themes.
Identification of causal effects of electoral rules is imperfect in the cross-country evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm-heterogeneity models changed how trade economists think about who trades, who gains and who loses, and about selection and reallocation. The Melitz (2003) model is a workhorse, and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI extended it. The framework led to a large body of empirical work on firm-level data and shaped trade policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the main originator of the framework. Helpman is a broader theorist of trade (increasing returns, firm organisation) and a co-author of the key extensions. Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, and Redding, are close contributors, so credit is somewhat shared.
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than two decades of confirmation, with many empirical tests and refinements.
uncertainties: Credit partly overlaps with Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum.
Krugman's earlier prize covers part of the new trade theory lineage.
Welfare conclusions depend on distributional assumptions such as Pareto productivity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation (BLP) and dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) give a way to measure market power, welfare and merger effects with real data. Competition policy and applied industrial organisation use them routinely. They changed both academic practice and antitrust and regulatory analysis.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes share credit for the BLP method. Pakes is also central to the dynamic-games work. Bresnahan, Reiss and Benkard have strong claims on related contributions, so the three-name limit is constraining.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The methods date from the 1990s and are used extensively in academia and in agencies, courts and industry.
uncertainties: Cost of choosing among Bresnahan, Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn.
Sensitivity of structural results to functional-form and equilibrium assumptions.
Industrial organisation methods are less directly tied to broad social questions than some alternatives.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work links optimal tax theory to evidence by using sufficient statistics, bunching estimators and the elasticity of taxable income. It changed how the profession estimates behavioural responses to taxation and informs real tax design debates. Quasi-experimental methods in a policy-relevant setting are central to it.
assessment.attribution: Saez is central (optimal top rates, bunching, ETI evidence). Chetty developed the sufficient-statistics approach and applications. Slemrod is an earlier ETI and tax-compliance contributor. Feldstein's seminal ETI paper is not creditable because he is deceased. Stantcheva and others are younger contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for the Saez, Slemrod and early Chetty work. Chetty's more recent work is still being evaluated. Some of the empirical elasticity estimates remain contested.
uncertainties: Credit is split across several people and overlaps with the inequality and mobility candidates.
Reliability of ETI estimates, which depend on design and on tax avoidance versus real responses.
Chetty's contributions span several lines, which complicates assignment of credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underlies modern central-bank analysis. Woodford provided its integrated theoretical foundation, Gali its empirical and policy applications, and Taylor the monetary policy rule. Its practical influence on inflation targeting and policy design is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is dispersed over many contributors: Calvo, Rotemberg, Clarida-Gali-Gertler, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Smets-Wouters and others. Any three-person selection is partly arbitrary. Bernanke already received a prize for other work.
assessment.maturity: Mature. It has been in use for roughly three decades, though the post-2021 inflation episode reopened debate on some assumptions.
uncertainties: Dispersed credit among many contributors.
Contested empirical fit of the standard NK model, especially after the recent inflation.
Taylor's rule is as much a policy prescription as a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence and theory on reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion explained behaviour in bargaining, public goods and contracts that standard self-interest models could not. The Fehr-Schmidt model made social preferences a tractable tool. The work reached incentives, contract theory and labour markets.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the leading experimental and conceptual figure, and Fehr-Schmidt is the key theory paper. Bolton-Ockenfels is a closely competing formulation. Falk and Rabin have related contributions. The lineage is shared with earlier behavioural and experimental prizes.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than 25 years of confirmation. Questions remain about external validity and the stability of preferences.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior behavioural and experimental prizes (Kahneman, Smith, Thaler).
Credit relative to Bolton-Ockenfels and Rabin.
Robustness of lab-based findings in field settings and the replication record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technology and the China-shock studies of local labour-market adjustment changed understanding of wage inequality, polarisation and trade's distributional costs. The empirical design uses exposure-based quasi-experimental variation with administrative-style data. It is influential in policy debates.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across both strands. Hanson and Dorn are co-authors of the trade-shock work. Katz, Acemoglu and Levy-Murnane are important to the task and skill-bias lineage, and Acemoglu has already won, so the credit structure is complicated.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The China-shock findings are well replicated, but the long-run interpretation (persistence, adjustment margins) and the shift-share methodology are still debated.
uncertainties: Concerns about shift-share identification and long-run interpretation.
Credit shared with Katz, Acemoglu and others.
Possible overlap with recent prizes on technology and labour markets.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic factor models and diffusion indexes made it possible to forecast and measure macroeconomic activity from large datasets. The work is methodologically deep and widely used by central banks and forecasters. It is influential, though less transformative for general economic understanding than the higher-ranked candidates.
assessment.attribution: Stock and Watson are the primary developers of diffusion indexes and of the forecasting framework. Forni-Hallin-Lippi-Reichlin, Diebold-Mariano and West developed related methods and forecast-evaluation tests. Credit is shared across several groups.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with around 25 years of use. The methods are standard, though newer machine-learning forecasting competes with them.
uncertainties: Competing credit with the European factor-model group and forecast-evaluation authors.
Whether the prize committee views forecasting methods as sufficiently consequential for economic science.
Overlap of Stock's work on weak instruments and structural VARs with other econometrics candidates.
